And then he received his PhD in artificial intelligence from the University of Edinburgh in 1978. His doctoral research was focused on how the human brain might represent knowledge and perform learning—topics deeply rooted in cognitive science and early computational neuroscience. These new artificial neural networks were still primitive by today’s standards—slow to train, limited in scale, and dependent on modest datasets. But they captured a radical possibility: that learning didn’t require encoding knowledge by hand. It might instead emerge from exposure, feedback, and the adjustment of connections over time. Much in the same way that we learned that our DNA does not pass on knowledge specifics so much as a learning infrastructure. For a moment, optimism surged. But the technology was ahead of its time. Computing power was limited, and the available data was insufficient to demonstrate the neural networks’ full potential. Once again, progress stalled. Public interest waned, funding dried up, and by the early 1990s, artificial intelligence entered its second major winter. But behind the scenes, something quiet was happening: Computing power was accelerating, data access was multiplying because of the internet, and researchers—many working in the margins—continued to refine the architectures and ideas that would eventually lead to a profound resurgence. The seeds of deep learning had been planted. They just needed time to grow. But as computing power exploded, things began to change. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 7 Emergent Intelligence Beyond Biology The internet began generating oceans of digital data. Graphics Processing Units or GPUs—originally designed for the high-speed rendering required in video game graphics—turned out to be perfect for parallel processing in neural networks. Unlike Central Processing Units or CPUs, which excel at a few complex operations at a time, GPUs run thousands of simple operations in parallel—the exact pattern needed to train large neural nets efficiently. By far the leader in this space is the Wall Street darling, NVIDIA, which recently ballooned into one of the world’s most valuable companies as others worked to catch up. NVIDIA Provides the Engine of AI Founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, NVIDIA began as a niche graphics card manufacturer focused on the emerging video game market. What set the company apart wasn’t just hardware—it was vision. Huang, who immigrated from Taiwan and worked as a dishwasher in his youth, has often said that what matters isn’t the job but how you do the job. He describes his desire in that job to be the best dishwasher ever. That relentless pursuit of excellence—combined with long-range thinking—became the cultural backbone of the company. Under Huang’s leadership, NVIDIA made a critical bet: that the same GPU chips used to accelerate graphics rendering for gamers could be repurposed for general purpose parallel processing. It was a bold move at the time, but it proved visionary. By the 2010s, as machine learning began to explode, it became clear that neural networks required vast amounts of parallel computation. NVIDIA’s GPUs were perfectly suited. Seemingly overnight, NVIDIA wasn’t just a gaming chip company—it became the default provider of AI infrastructure. Today, NVIDIA powers everything from autonomous vehicles to supercomputers to generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT. Its stock price soared, and Huang has become one of the most admired leaders in tech. Geoffrey Hinton, the “Godfather of AI” Back to Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, often called the Godfather of AI, who spent decades championing neural networks even when the field dismissed them, eventually leading to the breakthrough that ignited modern AI. He didn’t just imagine machines that could compute—he imagined machines that could learn in ways inspired by biology. His persistence paid off with AlexNet. In 2012, AlexNet, the system built by Hinton and his students, crushed the ImageNet visual recognition challenge using a deep convolutional neural network. It was the spark that reignited the field. Later recruited by Google, Hinton’s work laid the conceptual and architectural foundation for today’s deep learning systems. The breakthrough wasn’t about better logic. It was about brute force learning: Show a network millions of examples, let it make billions of mistakes, and it will eventually predict with uncanny accuracy. The success of AlexNet led directly to Google’s acquisition of DeepMind, the development of systems such as AlphaGo, and the modern deep learning revolution. What changed? The model, yes. But more than that, it was the injection of large amounts of energy and access to massive data using this incredible layered learning architecture idea, which originally evolved in the human brain under the shaping force of energy constraint. Early AI models failed in part because they didn’t mimic how we learn. But they also failed because they were underpowered—literally. Today’s deep neural networks are not just intelligent because they are more elegant and leverage how our brains learn. They are also intelligent because they are fueled. They draw on massive computational resources to radically scale the kind of localized pattern recognition our brains perform with a fraction of the energy. Human Memory Storage and AI Vector Databases As we encounter new experiences, observations, or facts and process them in a sequence of escalating layers of prediction and response, the hippocampus is engaged to determine when something new has occurred that should be updated in the memory system. And the new data only gets to the hippocampus if it contradicts expectations all the way up the chain. The filtering is the continuous discarding of all the lower, faster levels of prediction and response. But here’s a notable part: Most things are not stored. The hippocampus must make constant value judgments about the new information’s future worth. The brain is constantly filtering—deciding which inputs merit energy investment for long-term encoding.
